title: Three.js vs Godot
author: abdosarmini92
selftext:
What are you using to vibe code your games? Game engines are more reliable but Three.js is just faster in development. 

I made a quick test with matching prompts, one is using Three.js and the other used Godot. The Godot version took 2x the time and used %70 more message tokens. Which is a huge difference. 

Three.js is perfect for vibe coding but I want people that successfully managed to deploy games to Steam with it. 

What's your opinion?

comments.author: Low-Yellow-1521
comments.body:
always godot if u want to make an actual game

three.js is horrible for making actual games because it isnt a game engine. its only good for simple prototypes/demos

replies.author: abdosarmini92
replies.body: I mean there are real games made with it like this [one](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5527800/No_Asteroids/)

replies.author: Low-Yellow-1521
replies.body:
i never said its impossible to make a real game

i just said that using godot is better in every aspect

comments.author: AdHom
comments.body: The only reason I prefer Unity is because it's easier for me to work in myself, especially for animation work. If you're strictly vibecoding in headless I do think Godot is probably the all around better option but idk

comments.author: AdHom
comments.body: There are a ton of reasons you would not want to make a browser game, which is what three.js is useful for. Once you get past small, tech demo scale games you could run into a lot of issues. It's certainly impressive what can be done in the browser these days though

comments.author: youtpout
comments.body: Three.js for the web, godot for anything else

comments.author: kamilr641
comments.body: did you run the godot test with the same model and agent setup, and could it see the editor or run the game headless? if it had to guess at scene errors without feedback that could explain the extra time and tokens

replies.author: abdosarmini92
replies.body: same everything. headless godot. it faced some errors and it took longer to fix them than three.js. also it opened the game couple of times to test it live unlike three.js where it can test it in the background i guess

replies.author: kamilr641
replies.body: did it open the game by itself or was that in your prompt?

replies.author: kamilr641
replies.body: ok so it launched the game on its own. that could be part of the extra time, each launch and reading the output back is more steps than three.js needed. did it do that after every fix or just a few times?

comments.author: throwaway275275275
comments.body: I don't get why three.js is faster, a game engine is supposed to do more work for you than a browser, meaning less scripts/data to implement something, so less tokens to output, what can cause the difference in speed ?

comments.author: _HoundOfJustice
comments.body:
Actually Godot is the worst of the big 3. Unity and Unreal Engine have many features and perks that Godot lacks and/or has to be built by hand.

On top of that Unity and Unreal Engine both go "all in" into AI so they are not lacking behind Godot here either. For certain games Godot is ofc a easier choice, but generally Unity and Unreal have major advantages except for Godot being completely and always free and lightweight compared to other two.

comments.author: Gigaslavx
comments.body: Three is great for small demos but I say you mostly learning ai and there's close to no commerical success. Godot is not too bad quite limiting bit ok for small games but then once again so much mediocre small games. If not striving for realism as beginner stick to unity, otherwise you're just having fun which is alright I guess just don't take it too seriously thinking it's the next GTA

comments.author: Another_3
comments.body:
Remember three.js is one library, not an engine. 
Also faster not equals better

comments.author: Mockcomic
comments.body: Instead of threejs you could go with Babylon.js which is a web based game engine that Microsoft acquired/made. Wrap the application with electron or tauri(I recommend electron). Sign the application via Microsoft Azure using the pipeline electron has setup so it’s a trusted application.

comments.author: Kingnorik
comments.body: Check my 3js engine. I find I beat godot in ease of use. And my testing puts my engine at up to 60% less token use than normal 3js by it self. Free and everything. I literally made it for my own workflow. [In-Gen](http://gengaming.net)

comments.author: CaptainAlexWest
comments.body: I used three.js and I ended up making it into a custom editor and engine. Then I stopped and went to a real engine like unreal engine etc.

comments.author: Demien19
comments.body: Open sourced doesn't mean better (usually never does...).

replies.author: AdminClown
replies.body: It is better on the exact things that I mentioned. Complete control and ownership of your game and the ability to tinker with the engine.

replies.author: Demien19
replies.body: You will waste a lot of time tinkering instead of making game. And ownership... you still own your game unless you exceed license limitations, but when you do it - you just follow rules, nothing magical there.
